title: Data Newsroom
tagline: You ask questions of a table of data. Then you decide if a headline is true.
objectives: Write a rule with a column, a sign and a number or a word, and read how many rows it keeps.
Join two rules with AND, which needs both, or OR, which needs one.
Use BETWEEN to keep every number from one end to the other, both ends in.
Use NOT to keep the rows a rule would leave out.
Say whether the numbers back a headline, and if not, why: too few people, only the best bit, the numbers say no, one did not cause the other.

opening.line1: Today you find out if a headline is telling the truth.
opening.line2: You check it against the facts it came from.
opening.line3: Social media, adverts and the news tell you things every day. Some of those things are not true.

story.b1: Fionn, our reporter, has gone home sick. He wrote six headlines and nobody has checked them.
story.b2: The paper prints at midnight. Nothing prints without a check.
story.b3: You are on the night desk tonight. The facts are in a table of data. You ask the table questions. Then you stamp each headline PRINT or SPIKE. PRINT sends it to the paper. SPIKE throws it out.

facts.intro: Fionn put his facts in two tables: grids of rows and columns. Every headline tonight comes from one of them.
facts.t1: 60 people of Rathmore answered a survey.
facts.t1cols: age · area · phone hours · sleep hours · exam score · café visits · pet · bus stars
facts.t2: Table two holds 92 summer days at the harbour.
facts.t2cols: date · temperature · rain · visitors · ice creams sold · sea rescues

tour.s1: This is the table. It has sixty people. Each person is one row.
tour.s2: This is the question box. Type a rule here, then press Enter. A rule is a question for the table. The table keeps only the rows that fit your rule.
tour.s3: This is the count. It tells you how many rows are left.

c1.title: The question
c1.headline: Eight hours of sleep lifts exam scores
c1.show1: A rule has a column, a sign and a number.
c1.show2: age is the column. < means less than. It keeps people under 20.
c1.show3: A rule is also called a query.
c1.ask: Keep only the people who slept eight hours or more.
c1.h1: The column is sleep_hours. The sign for eight or more is >=.
c1.h2: Write the column, then the sign, then the number: sleep_hours, then >=, then 8.

judge.ok: Showing 17 of 60. Seventeen people slept eight hours or more.
judge.wrong: Your rule shows {got} rows, but it should show 17. Check the sign.

options: No. The people who slept eight hours or more scored lower.
c1.right: Right. The numbers say the opposite.
c1.wrong: Look again. The people who slept eight hours or more scored lower, not higher.
c1.stampShow2: Dee stamped it SPIKE, meaning do not print.
c1.stampShow3: Her reason was too few people. Every stamp needs a reason.
c1.stampAsk: Your turn. Stamp it, then pick a reason.
c1.stampOk: SPIKE. The numbers say no. People who slept eight hours or more scored 61.0. Everyone else scored 65.3.
c1.stampNo: Look at the two averages. Which group scored higher?
c1.reasonNo: Seventeen people is enough to check. The averages show the headline is wrong.
c1.doneLine: One headline checked. Five are left.
c1.stampShowCard: Harbour café is the town favourite

c2.title: Two at once
c2.headline: Most Rathmore teens are on their phones five hours a day
c2.show1: AND joins two rules. It keeps a row only when both are true.
c2.show2: This keeps teens with a dog: 3 of 60.
c2.show3: Words go in quotes. Numbers do not.
c2.ask: Keep teens who use their phone five hours or more.
c2.h1: For teens, use age < 20. For five hours or more, use phone_hours >= 5.
c2.h2: Put AND between the two rules.

judge.ok: Showing 6 of 60. Six of the 18 teens use their phone that much.
judge.wrong: Your rule shows {got} rows, but it should show 6. Check both rules.

c2.right: Right. Six of eighteen is one in three.
c2.wrong: Six of eighteen is one in three. One in three is not most.
c2.stampAsk: Now stamp it, with a reason.
c2.stampOk: SPIKE. The numbers say no: 6 of 18 is not most.
c2.stampNo: Only six of the eighteen teens use their phone that much. Is that most?
c2.reasonNo: Eighteen teens are enough people to check. The problem is that Fionn wrote "most". Six of 18 is not most.

c3.title: One week
c3.headline: Rathmore harbour gets 3,000 visitors a day
c3.show1: BETWEEN keeps rows from one number to another. Rows at both numbers are kept too.
c3.show2: This rule keeps 16 days, from 20 to 22 degrees.
c3.show3: Each row here is one summer day.
c3.ask: Fionn only looked at days 40 to 46. Keep those days.
c3.h2: Write day_no, then BETWEEN, then the first day, then AND, then the last day.

judge.ok: Showing 7 of 92 days. These 7 days are regatta week, 10 to 16 July. That is the week of the harbour boat races.
judge.wrong: Your rule shows {got} days, but it should show 7. Check both ends.

c3.compare1: Those 7 days had 3,158 visitors a day.
c3.compare2: All 92 days had 2,215 visitors a day.
options: Took the best week and called it the summer.
He did nothing wrong. 3,000 is the right number.
c3.right: Right. One good week is not the whole summer.
c3.wrong: He took the best week and called it the summer.
c3.stampAsk: Now stamp it, with a reason.
c3.stampOk: SPIKE. Fionn used only the best week. Regatta week is not the whole summer.
c3.stampNo: Fionn used seven days out of 92. Can seven days show the whole summer?
c3.reasonNo: The numbers for that week are true. The problem is that Fionn picked the best week.

c4.title: Either one
c4.headline: More than half of Rathmore people have a dog or a cat
c4.show1: OR keeps a row when either rule is true.
c4.show2: This keeps the 30 people in Marsh or Hill.
c4.show3: Each side of OR is a whole rule, with its own column and sign.
c4.ask: Keep everyone with a dog or a cat.
c4.h1: The column is pet. Words go in quotes: "dog".
c4.h2: Type pet = "dog" OR pet = "cat". Each side is a full rule.

judge.ok: Showing 31 of 60. That is more than half.
judge.wrong: Your rule shows {got} rows, but it should show 31. Write a full rule on each side of OR.

c4.wrong: Thirty-one of sixty is over half. This one is true.
c4.stampAsk: Now stamp it, with a reason.
c4.stampOk: PRINT. The numbers back it: 31 of 60.
c4.stampNo: Not every headline is wrong. 31 of 60 is over half.
c4.reasonNo: This headline is true. The reason to print is that the numbers back it.

c5.title: Leave out
c5.headline: Outside Old Town, everyone loves the new bus
c5.show1: NOT reverses a rule. It keeps the rows the rule would throw out.
c5.show2: This keeps the 44 people who are not in Old Town.
c5.ask: Keep people outside Old Town who gave the bus any stars.
c5.h1: For outside Old Town, use NOT area = "Old Town". For any stars, use bus_stars > 0.

judge.ok: Showing 4 of 60. Four people rated the bus at all.
judge.wrong: Your rule shows {got} rows, but it should show 4. Type NOT first. Then type AND between the two rules.

c5.compare2: The other 40 people outside Old Town did not rate the bus.
c5.right: Right. Four people cannot tell us what all 44 think.
c5.wrong: Four people rated it. They cannot tell us what all 44 think.
c5.stampAsk: Now stamp it, with a reason.
c5.stampOk: SPIKE. The reason is too few people. Only 4 of the 44 people outside Old Town rated the bus.
c5.stampNo: Only four of the 44 people rated the bus. Is that enough for "everyone"?
c5.reasonNo: The four did love it. There are just too few of them.

c6.title: The rush
c6.headline: Ice cream sales cause sea rescues
c6.ring: This is Dee. One headline is left. The printing press starts in three minutes. If time runs out, the paper prints Fionn’s headline as he wrote it.
c6.intro: Fionn says more ice creams mean more sea rescues. Check the hot days, then the cold days.
c6.ask1: Keep the hot days: 24 degrees or more.

judge1.ok: Showing 27 of 92 days. An average hot day had 290 ice creams sold and 2.8 sea rescues.
judge1.wrong: Your rule shows {got} days, but it should show 27. Check the sign.

c6.ask2: Now keep the days under 18 degrees.

judge2.ok: Showing 28 of 92 days. An average cold day had 91 ice creams sold and 0.5 sea rescues.
judge2.wrong: Your rule shows {got} days, but it should show 28. Check the sign.

c6.stampOk: SPIKE. Ice cream did not cause the rescues. Hot weather caused the sales and the rescues.
c6.stampNo: Ice cream sales and sea rescues both rise on hot days. Does one cause the other, or does the heat cause both?
c6.reasonNo: The numbers are real, and there are enough days. The problem is that the headline says ice cream causes the rescues. Could something else cause both the sales and the rescues?
c6.timeUp: It is midnight and time is up. The press printed Fionn’s headline on page one.
c6.printedLine: The press printed Fionn’s headline. It is on page one.
c6.letter1: Dear Editor, I sell ice cream at the harbour.
c6.letter2: Your paper blamed my cones for three rescues.
c6.letter3: On hot days, more people swim and buy ice cream.
c6.letter4: The heat caused the rescues, not my cones. Marie Byrne.
c6.fixAsk: Stamp it again. Pick the right reason this time.
c6.fixOk: You fixed the stamp. The heat caused the ice cream sales and the sea rescues. All your work is still saved.
c6.doneLine: Six headlines checked. The press is printing the paper now.
c6.compare1: Hot days averaged 290 ice creams and 2.8 rescues a day.
c6.compare2: Cold days averaged 91 ice creams and 0.5 rescues a day.

front.rename: Type your name for the page

badges.name: The rush
badges.line: You finished before the press started.

recap: A query asks a table a question.
AND needs both rules to match. OR needs just one.
Before you print a headline, check that the numbers really back it.

close.exitDone: You have finished the last five questions.

felt: I can write a rule with AND, OR or NOT.
I can say what BETWEEN keeps.
I can say why a headline gets spiked.
close.freeIntro: Here are two more headlines from Fionn. Check them with your own rules.

free.headline: Harbour people visit the café most
free.hint: Try area = "Harbour" and read the café average.
free.reveal: People who live in Harbour average 7.9 café visits. Everyone else averages 7.4. These are almost the same, so Dee spikes the headline.

free.headline: Rain keeps the visitors away
free.hint: Try rain_mm > 5, then rain_mm = 0. Read the visitors average.
free.reveal: Wet days had 1,846 visitors a day. Dry days had 2,559. The numbers back the headline, so Dee prints it.
